title: Scientific Theories
short: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation that ties together many facts and observations, like the cell theory and the theory of evolution. A law describes a pattern; a theory explains it.
trouble: Students think "theory" means a guess, as in everyday speech, and that a theory becomes a law once proved. Theories and laws are different kinds of ideas; a theory is among the strongest kinds of scientific knowledge.

blocks.html: In everyday talk, "it's just a theory" means "it's just a guess." In science, the word means almost the opposite. Knowing the difference helps you read about biology, from cells to evolution.

A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation that ties together many facts and observations. A scientific law describes a pattern, often in a sentence or an equation, without explaining why it happens. A theory does not turn into a law when it is "proved"; they are different kinds of ideas.

head: Kind of idea
What it is
Example
rows: This onion cell has a nucleus.
A testable explanation for a narrow question
If yeast is warmed to 35 °C, then it will make gas faster than at 20 °C.
A description of a pattern that always holds under stated conditions
Matter is not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
A broad, well-tested explanation that ties many observations together
The cell theory; the theory of evolution; the germ theory of disease.

blocks.html: A theory earns its place by surviving many tests, by many people, using different methods. The cell theory is an example. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden concluded that plants are made of cells; in 1839 Theodor Schwann extended the idea to animals; in 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that every cell comes from an existing cell. Since then, every living thing examined has fit. The theory of evolution is supported in the same way, by fossils, anatomy, DNA and selection seen happening today.

blocks.title: Which kind of idea?
blocks.q: Sort these: (a) "All living things are made of cells, and cells come from other cells." (b) "The leaves on this plant are turning yellow." (c) "If the plant lacks nitrogen, then adding nitrogen will turn new leaves green."
steps: (c) is an if-then explanation for one plant that a test could support or refute: a hypothesis.
(a) is a broad explanation tested on every kind of living thing: a theory (the cell theory).

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Every cell comes from an existing cell, and all living things are made of cells.
cards.why: The cell theory explains a huge body of observations.

cards.text: The bread dough doubled in size in an hour.
If salt water slows seed sprouting, then seeds in 2% salt water will sprout more slowly than seeds in tap water.
Living things share common ancestors, and populations change over generations by natural selection and other processes.
cards.why: The theory of evolution ties together fossils, anatomy, DNA and observed change.

cards.text: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
cards.why: A law describes what always happens; it does not say why.

cards.text: Many diseases are caused by microorganisms that spread from host to host.

blocks.cap: Sort each statement. Tap a card, then a group.

blocks.html: Thinking "theory" means a guess, and that a theory becomes a law once it is proved. A hypothesis is the tentative idea; a theory is among the strongest kinds of scientific knowledge. Laws describe; theories explain. Like all of science, a theory can still be revised when new evidence comes in, and that openness is part of its strength.
